units.text: Let's follow one notification that several systems need. The producer publishes once to a topic rather than calling each consumer. S N S takes responsibility for forwarding a copy to each eligible subscription.

An endpoint can handle a notification quickly, or a queue can hold the copy until that consumer is ready. Choose based on what happens if a consumer is unavailable, not just whether it can receive the first message.

One event can feed independent subscribers without the producer managing their individual addresses or schedules. If one consumer slows down, a queue on that particular branch can absorb its backlog without making the publisher wait for that work to finish.

A publish acknowledgment means S N S accepted the message; it doesn't mean every subscriber finished. Observe delivery and failure at the subscription, then inspect the receiving application's processing separately.

The same topic can route two kinds of notification. A filter on message attributes reads the separate metadata the publisher sent. A body-scoped filter instead matches fields in a valid Jason body. Use the scope that actually contains the field.

A matching subscription gets its copy. A nonmatching subscription gets nothing, and that is expected routing rather than failure. Test a known match and nonmatch after a policy change has had time to propagate.

Publish to a topic when several eligible subscriptions should see the event. For an individual mobile device, publish to its platform endpoint. The device registration and valid platform endpoint matter; an accepted send is not proof the user saw the notification.

A service can also publish notifications when supported and configured. Check that the source supports the destination and that the topic policy lets the intended source publish. Don't open the whole topic to get one integration working.

Let's separate permission to publish from encryption at rest. The caller needs permission to publish to the topic; the topic policy matters for access by others. With a customer managed K M S key, the key policy must also allow the appropriate publisher or service use.

Encryption protects stored S N S messages, not a substitute for authorization. Verify the intended publisher, topic policy, key permissions, and subscription delivery independently. A successful publish isn't proof that a queue accepted delivery.

Each queue gets its own copy when delivery is allowed. Let the S N S service send only from the intended topic in the queue policy. That policy is distinct from a worker's permission to receive or delete messages.

Suppose inventory keeps up but analytics is slow. Its queue buffers that branch's copy without holding inventory back. Monitor each backlog and distinguish a failed S N S delivery from a delivered message that failed during worker processing.

An object-created event can publish to a supported Standard S N S topic. Give each downstream consumer its own queue if each needs a copy. An S three notification delivered directly to one queue doesn't create a separate copy for every application.

Use EventBridge when you need richer rules or a different target set. S three does not deliver direct event notifications to an S Q S fye foe queue; an EventBridge route can target fye foe where appropriate. Choose the route by the target and its requirements.

Let's follow published records into a destination that receives batches. The S N S subscription assumes a role that can write to the intended Firehose stream. The delivery stream has its own configuration and permissions for writing to the final destination.

Firehose buffers records before delivering them. If records don't appear where expected, first check S N S delivery to the stream, then check stream metrics and destination delivery. A successful publish doesn't tell you which later hop worked.

Publish related events under the same message group. A subscribed fye foe queue can retain that per-group order; a Standard queue does not give that guarantee. Different groups can make progress independently.

Deduplication can suppress repeats within the applicable scope and window. A subscription filter deliberately omits events that don't match. Don't assume that every subscriber receives every event, or that the application no longer needs idempotent writes.

We'll route a business event without hard-coding its consumers. The producer puts an event on a bus. Matching rules choose what targets receive it. The event describes something that happened; the rules decide what happens next.

Target delivery and consumer processing are different outcomes. A matching rule selects the target; then delivery must succeed. The target may still have its own work and failure handling after it receives the event.

A bus receives events. The default bus receives supported A W S service events. A custom bus can hold application events with its own rules, and a partner bus receives events from an authorized partner source.

Match meaningful fields like the source and detail type so an order-created handler doesn't receive an unrelated event. Several matching rules can route the same event. If nothing matches, inspect the actual event fields before changing the target.

A rule might match correctly while the target is temporarily unavailable. The target retry policy bounds how long and how often EventBridge retries delivery. A permanent permission failure isn't repaired by increasing the retry count.

A configured rule-target dead-letter queue can preserve undelivered events. Inspect the error and fix the target problem before reprocessing. That queue doesn't capture an application error after the target already accepted the event.

The receiving account grants the intended source permission in its event bus resource policy. Restrict permitted principals or conditions to what the integration needs. Sharing the name of a bus does not authorize a sender.

The sending side also needs authority to put events on the destination bus. In this direct publish example, check the application’s identity permission. Then verify a receiving rule matches the event and can deliver it to its local target.

Let's recover missed work without asking producers to recreate events. An archive retains events from its source bus, optionally restricted by an event pattern. Pick retention so that your recovery window is still available when you need it.

Replay a selected window to the original bus, optionally to selected rules. Replaying doesn't remove the archive. A consumer may already have handled an event, so make reprocessing safe and verify the result instead of blindly applying side effects again.

A schema tells a consumer which fields and types to expect. Discovery can infer schemas from observed events, and a new shape can create a new version. Compare versions before rolling out a producer change.

A generated binding helps application code read the shape. The schema is a contract aid, not automatic validation or a delivery rule. Keep old consumers compatible, and test a representative event against the rule and the consumer.

Use Scheduler when the clock should trigger work even when no event arrives. A rate repeats by interval, cron expresses calendar timing, and a one-time schedule targets a specific time. Choose the appropriate time zone for calendar schedules.

Scheduler needs its own permission to invoke the target. Choose the allowed timing window and configure retry and failure handling where needed. Verify the target received the scheduled call; scheduling it doesn't prove processing completed.

Pipes connects a source to a target without a custom polling function for every integration. The filter decides which source records continue. For example, select orders that need fulfillment rather than forwarding every event.

Enrich matching records only if the target needs more context, then deliver them with the configured permissions. Check the particular source and target behavior for batching and retries. A pipe is a point-to-point integration, not automatically a fanout bus.
